## Discussion

This chapter does not aim to provide a definitive validation of
source-reconstructed HD-EEG against intracranial EEG. Rather, it asks
whether large-scale regional spectral organisation is sufficiently
preserved to support cautious comparison, whether separating oscillatory
and broadband components changes that comparison, and whether the
broadband estimates themselves are stable across methodological choices.
The chapter is therefore evaluated not by whether it eliminates all
ambiguity, but by whether it makes the sources of ambiguity explicit and
tests their consequences.

The posterior-to-anterior frequency gradient recovered here is consistent
with reports from MEG using both parameterised (Mahjoory et al. 2020) and
non-parametric data-driven (Arana et al. 2026) approaches, and from iEEG
using spectral parameterisation (Kalamangalam et al. 2020). The partial
preservation of this gradient in HD-EEG extends the pattern across an
additional modality and a coarser spatial resolution regime.

<!-- FIX #7: tied the Jensen and Bonnefond observation to the specific
H1 finding it supports (the cross-modal recovery of alpha), rather than
letting it float as a free-standing remark on circuit architecture. -->
The cross-modal recovery of alpha specifically (Section 3.1.3) is
consistent with alpha being tied to laminar and feedback/feedforward
circuit architecture (Jensen and Bonnefond 2026), implying that at least
some of the regional oscillatory structure recovered here reflects broader
circuit organisation rather than isolated narrowband generators.

###  Methodological caveats and limitations

<!-- FIX #8: added a signposting sentence to orient the reader through
the limitations, and reordered the paragraphs to follow that grouping
(data-level → method-level → inferential). Previous version listed six
limitations in a flat sequence without grouping. -->
The limitations of this chapter fall into three groups: data-level
constraints on the comparison itself, methodological dependencies of the
parameterisation, and limits on what can be inferred from convergence
across metrics.

**Data-level.** <!-- FIX #3 (cont.): the full eye-state limitation that
was previously duplicated in §1 now lives only here. -->
The Frauscher iEEG atlas was recorded with eyes closed, whereas the
HD-EEG dataset was recorded with eyes open. Eye state affects oscillatory
activity, most strongly posterior alpha power, and may also affect
aperiodic exponent and offset (Geller et al. 2014). Where cross-modal
agreement is observed, it is therefore observed despite differences in
recording condition. Where cross-modal agreement is weak, modality and
condition cannot be fully separated with the data used here.

The data aggregation structures also differ between modalities: 1772
channels across 106 patients in iEEG versus 1444 virtual sensors across
19 subjects in HD-EEG. Per-region statistics in iEEG aggregate across
patients within channels, while per-region HD-EEG statistics aggregate
across virtual sensors within subjects then across subjects. This
asymmetry should be considered when interpreting between-region
differences.

The Frauscher atlas was further recorded in patients with refractory
epilepsy. Although only channels in non-epileptogenic regions were
retained, the extent to which spectral features generalise to non-epileptic
populations is a known limitation of this reference (Frauscher et al.
2018).

**Method-level.** Spectral parameterisation depends on several modelling
choices, including the assumed aperiodic functional form, the fitting
frequency range, and peak detection thresholds; results should be
interpreted with caution (Donoghue et al. 2021). The chapter addresses
this dependency directly through the stability analyses of §3.3.

A subset of source-reconstructed spectra additionally exhibited near-flat
spectral slopes with exponents close to zero and low model fit quality
(R² < 0.70). These spectra typically showed no clear 1/f structure and,
where peaks were present, these were confined to the beta range. Such
profiles are unlikely to reflect genuine neural dynamics with an unusually
flat broadband component. More plausibly, they arise from source labels
that receive little coherent neural signal after inverse modelling, so
that the reconstructed time course is dominated by spatially smoothed
noise or leakage from neighbouring regions (Tait et al. 2021). Recent
biophysical modelling suggests that high-frequency broadband power in
scalp EEG may not be neural in origin (Brake and Khadra 2025; Brake et al.
2024), and this concern extends to source-reconstructed data, where the
inverse solution cannot recover signal that was not present at the sensor
level. Fitting specparam's fixed aperiodic model to such spectra produces
nominally valid parameter estimates, but these should not be interpreted
as reflecting cortical broadband dynamics (Wilson et al. 2024; Gerster et
al. 2022). Sources with R² below 0.90 were flagged and the sensitivity
of regional results to their inclusion or exclusion is reported in
Section 3.2.1.

**Inferential.** The chapter reports convergence across multiple
comparison methods (Afnan overlap, Spearman across regions, peak-prevalence
differences, hierarchical Bayesian regression) rather than committing to
a single pipeline. Each metric encodes different assumptions about what
counts as agreement between modalities — whether one modality is treated
as ground truth, whether comparison is made at the level of medians or
full distributions, whether scale or rank is preserved. Convergence across
these metrics is reassuring but does not establish their interchangeability
under conditions where modalities diverge more sharply than they do here.
A systematic evaluation under controlled simulation, where the underlying
spatial pattern is known, would help characterise when different cross-modal
metrics agree and where they diverge, and is left for future work.

### Methodological caveats and limitations

Spectral parameterisation depends on several modelling choices, including the
assumed aperiodic functional form, the fitting frequency range, and peak
detection thresholds. Results should therefore be interpreted with caution

A subset of source-reconstructed spectra exhibited near-flat spectral slopes with exponents close to zero and low model fit quality (R² < 0.70). These spectra typically showed no clear 1/f structure and, where peaks were present, these were confined to the beta range. Such profiles are unlikely to reflect genuine neural dynamics with an unusually flat broadband component. More plausibly, they arise from source labels that receive little coherent neural signal after inverse modelling, so that the reconstructed time course is dominated by spatially smoothed noise or leakage from neighbouring regions [@tait2021SystematicEvaluationSource]. Recent biophysical modelling suggests that high-frequency broadband power in scalp EEG may not be neural in origin [@brake2025ContributionsActionPotentials; @brake2024NeurophysiologicalBasisAperiodic], and this concern extends to source-reconstructed data, where the inverse solution cannot recover signal that was not present at the sensor level. Fitting specparam's fixed aperiodic model to such spectra produces nominally valid parameter estimates, but these should not be interpreted as reflecting cortical broadband dynamics [@wilson2024ModelSelectionSpectral; @gerster2022SeparatingNeuralOscillations]. This chapter demonstrates <!-- TODO finalise once results are complete --> the
value of jointly examining oscillatory and aperiodic spectral features when
mapping regional brain activity. Regional spectral profiles show partial
preservation across iEEG and HD-EEG source-reconstructed recordings, suggesting
that large-scale spatial organisation is partly recoverable across modalities.
At the same time, accounting for the aperiodic background alters the
interpretation of oscillatory findings, highlighting the risk of conflating
broadband spectral variation with narrowband oscillations. These results
underscore the need for cautious, model-aware interpretation of parameterised
spectral measures in human EEG research.


An open question raised by this work concerns the evaluation of cross-modal comparison metrics themselves. Several reasonable choices were available here — Spearman correlation across regions, per-ROI distribution overlap, peak-prevalence differences — and each encodes different assumptions about what counts as agreement between modalities (whether one is treated as ground truth, whether comparison is made at the level of medians or full distributions, whether scale or rank is preserved). The convergence of results across these metrics in the present chapter is reassuring, but it does not establish their interchangeability under conditions where modalities diverge more sharply than they do here. A systematic evaluation under controlled simulation, where the underlying spatial pattern is known, would help characterise when different cross-modal metrics agree and where they diverge, and is left for future work.

The broader value of normative mapping in resting-state EEG lies less in its potential clinical applications than in its methodological role: source-reconstructed scalp EEG is now the dominant non-invasive tool for studying regional electrophysiology in cognitive and clinical neuroscience, yet its empirical validation against direct intracranial measurement has been carried out mostly with MEG [@afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource]. The contribution of the present chapter to that validation effort is specific in three ways. It uses HD-EEG rather than MEG, which is more widely available but more vulnerable to volume conduction and source mixing. It examines oscillatory and aperiodic features jointly rather than band power alone, as in earlier normative scalp-EEG maps [@janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping]. And it reports convergence across multiple comparison methods rather than committing to a single pipeline, which strengthens the conclusions where convergence holds and flags where it does not. The chapter does not claim that normative HD-EEG maps are ready for clinical biomarker use, nor that the patterns reported here generalise across populations, ages, or recording conditions; both questions require dedicated work. What it offers is a characterisation of which features of regional spectral organisation are recoverable from source-reconstructed HD-EEG, and which are sensitive to the assumptions of the analysis pipeline used here.

The posterior-to-anterior frequency gradient recovered here is consistent with reports from MEG using both parameterised [@mahjoory2020FrequencyGradientHuman] and non-parametric data-driven [@arana2026MEGLowdensityEEG] approaches, and from iEEG using spectral parameterisation [@kalamangalam2020NeurophysiologicalBrainMap]. Our finding that this gradient is partially preserved in HD-EEG extends the pattern across an additional modality and a coarser spatial resolution regime.
